title: Heat Pump Rebates in Hamilton 2026: Older Homes and Up to $7,500
desc: Hamilton heat pump rebates for 2026 under Home Renovation Savings: 61% of homes predate 1981, and rebates depend on your current heating fuel.
badge: Up to $7,500 for an air-source heat pump
lead: Hamilton has 222,810 households and 61% live in homes built before 1981. Older houses often combine radiators, baseboards or oil heat, which change the rebate.
cards_heading: What Home Renovation Savings pays for a heat pump in Hamilton
cards_intro: We re-read the program's heat pump page and its requirements document on October 3, 2026. No home energy assessment is needed for this stream, but a participating HVAC contractor and written pre-approval are.

cards.title: Air-source, electric, oil, propane or wood heat
cards.note: For a cold-climate air-source heat pump replacing electric resistance, oil, propane or wood as the main heat. A 3-ton system pays $3,750 and 6 tons or more reaches the cap.

cards.title: Air-source, Enbridge gas heat
cards.note: For homes primarily heated by an Enbridge gas furnace or boiler. The cap is reached at 4 tons.

cards.title: Ground-source
cards.note: For electric, oil, propane or wood homes. Gas homes get a flat $3,000. The system must be a full installation sized to the home's load.

cards.title: Rented heat pump
cards.note: Rentals are eligible for any primary heating fuel: $500 per ton for air-source, up to $2,000, or a flat $3,000 for ground-source.

cards.title: More than one outdoor unit
cards.amount: Up to three units, one rebate
cards.note: If several outdoor units are needed to heat the whole home, their tons add up and one rebate is paid on the total, for example 3 + 3 tons for $7,500.

cards.title: One rebate, pre-approved
cards.note: One rebate per home. The contractor needs written pre-approval before installing, files the post-installation application within 30 days, and the cheque arrives within 60 days of approval.

after_cards: The requirements document lists no end date, but the program's other streams close in late 2026, so check the program page before you sign a contract. Pre-approval is mandatory: an installation done first earns nothing.
sections: The 2021 Census counts 66,820 owner-occupied detached houses built before 1981 in Hamilton, 72% of households in an eligible house type and 66% owning. A house on baseboards, oil, propane or wood gets $1,250 per ton, up to $7,500. A gas house gets $500 per ton, up to $2,000.

An oil-heated Hamilton home must move to an electric heat pump and work with a TSSA-registered contractor to maintain, empty or remove the storage tank and piping. The owner signs an oil and propane tank removal attestation form, which goes with the pre-installation application. The rebate is not paid if the tank is left in service.

The system must be able to distribute heat throughout the whole conditioned space, including the basement if there is one. Older Hamilton houses with finished basements and no ducts need this addressed in the quote. Ask whether the plan uses ducted units, several indoor heads, or both.

The installed system must be capable of heating and cooling year-round, so a heating-only model is not eligible. That excludes some older designs and affects air-to-water systems, which the program does not accept.

Before approval the contractor submits photos of the existing heating system and its nameplate. For an electrically heated home that means the air handler or electric baseboards in at least three areas. For a wood-heated home it means the stove. Hamilton houses with several heating types should ask the contractor which system the program will treat as primary.

The rebate is paid on rated heating capacity at 8.3°C, not on the nameplate size a salesperson quotes. Ask the Hamilton contractor for the NRCan-listed capacity and divide by 12,000 BTU/h to get tons, so you can check the rebate yourself before the pre-installation application is filed.
claim_steps: Decide whether you are replacing oil, gas, baseboards or wood.
Confirm eligibility on the program's short form and get the list of participating HVAC contractors.
Choose a contractor from that list. Ask for a load calculation and the NRCan sizing tool form for each outdoor unit.
Wait for written pre-approval before any installation starts.
After the install, check that the contractor files the post-installation application within 30 days, with the final itemized invoice and photos.
faq: What happens with an oil tank?
It must be removed or emptied by a TSSA-registered contractor.
